newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Charity urges defence of Afghan women's rights.
newsitem.headline: Charity urges defence of Afghan women's rights.

text.p: Save the Children urged U.N. agencies, donor countries and other aid agencies on Sunday to unite in defence of the human rights of Afghan women and girls.

The U.S., British and Swedish branches of the charity said in a statement that they would have to suspend programmes in Afghanistan directly affected by what they called official restrictions on women's employment and girls' education.
The statement did not name the radical Islamic Taleban militia which banned most women from working and stopped girls from going to school after it captured Kabul on September 27.

"Our main programme was landmine education in all schools in Kabul," Andrew Wilder, Field Office Director for Save the Children USA, told Reuters. "We have had to suspend it because 70 percent of the teachers are women."

He said the programme was unlikely to be resumed before the end of the school year in about one month's time. "We are hoping that when the new school year begins in March-April, these (discriminatory) policies will change," he added.
Save the Children UK halted educational programmes in the Taleban-held western city of Herat in March for similar reasons.

The statement urged the international community to come together to ensure that Afghan women and girls had equal access to education, the right to a safe and secure environment, and the right of women to employment outside the home.

"Although every government has the right to legislate civil codes which respect the nature of their cultural and religious values, there are internationally-recognised basic human rights for males and females that should be respected by all parties within Afghanistan," Save the Children said.

"We strongly urge all Afghan parties to ensure equal opportunity for employment and education in order that all Afghans...may continue to actively participate in their country's development," it added.

The Taleban have told all women employees except health workers to stay at home until it decides how they can work without coming into contact with men. The movement also says the education system must be reorganised to segregate the sexes.
